title: Blessings for everything
hook: Scottish Highland blessings, collected as Carmina Gadelica, for kindling fire, milking, sleep

segments.voice: Yesterday, the encircling prayer: caim. Your line was circled by god. Where did you trace your circle before walking in? Day one thousand one hundred fifty.

Morning in a Highland cottage. Last night the fire was banked low, the embers covered over to keep them alive. Now someone kneels at the hearth with cold hands, uncovers the glow, adds fuel, and blows it back into flame. And while doing it, they say a blessing. Not in church. On their knees at the hearth, with the draft coming in under the door. A collector named Alexander Carmichael went around the Highlands and islands of Scotland writing down prayers like that, and he published them as Carmina Gadelica. Today: blessings for everything.

Carmina Gadelica is Latin for Gaelic songs. Inside are blessings for the jobs of an ordinary day. Kindling the fire in the morning. Banking it again at night. Milking the cow. Churning. Weaving cloth. Setting out on a journey. Lying down to sleep. Carmichael heard them from working people, and he printed the Gaelic beside his English, polishing some as he went. What stands out is that nothing is too small. The fire blessing doesn't wait for a holy moment; lighting the fire is the holy moment. The first letter to Timothy says it in the King James words: "every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving: For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer." Brother Lawrence turned his cake for the love of God. These blessings go a step further and give each chore its own words. Paul writes to the Colossians: "whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus." Whatsoever. The Gaelic blessings take that word at face value. In these prayers, Christ, Mary, the saints and the angels are invited into the cowshed, the kitchen and the boat. The fire at night is banked in God's name, so that the house is kept while everyone sleeps. The milking blessing turns a cold dawn chore into a moment of company. There's something practical here. A blessing ties attention to the job. It's hard to scroll a phone and bless the milking at the same time. And there's something tender, too: work nobody thanks you for, done in front of someone who sees it. The world in Carmichael's pages has changed. But kettles, dishes and commutes are chores too. The hearth has moved, and the habit can move with it.
screen: `A BLESSING TIES ATTENTION TO THE JOB.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless one daily chore. Pick a job you'll do today: the kettle, the dishes, the laundry, the drive. Hold it in mind now. See your hands doing it, step by step. If you pray, you can borrow the words from Colossians, whatsoever ye do, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, and ask God's blessing on that job when it comes. If you don't, decide to do it slowly, with full attention, as if it mattered. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Blessings for everything. The Gaelic habit, written down in Carmina Gadelica, of blessing the fire, the milking, the road and sleep.
Your line: bless the fire. Today, when you switch on the stove or the kettle, stop for one breath and bless it. Day one thousand one hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Some Christians today pray from Carmina Gadelica or from modern books of Celtic-style daily prayer, saying short blessings over chores, meals, journeys and sleep.

notes: No blessing from Carmina Gadelica is quoted; all are described. Confirm the list of occasions (kindling, smooring/banking, milking, churning, weaving, journeys, sleep) against the collection.
'Carmina Gadelica is Latin for Gaelic songs' is a gloss of the title (carmina = songs/hymns; Gadelica = Gaelic); confirm.
'He printed the Gaelic beside his English' describes Carmichael's parallel-text edition; confirm.
Invocation of Mary, the saints (including Bride/Brigid) and angels is described as in the texts, not commended; Protestant readers may differ on invoking saints. Confirm the framing.
Dates of collection and publication deliberately omitted under the claims rule.

Editor: 1 Corinthians 10:31 was already quoted on day 1138 (Brother Lawrence, the same holy-in-chores angle); replaced in teach, practice, match and myth with 1 Timothy 4:4–5 (KJV, confirm wording) and Colossians 3:17, and added a line naming Lawrence so the day builds on 1138 instead of repeating it (the Gaelic blessings give each chore its own words).

Auditor: added that Carmichael edited and polished some texts (teach and myth reveal); the editorial reshaping of Carmina Gadelica is well known to scholars, and the myth reveal had presented the texts as a straight record. Confirm wording.
